what_its_for: Vancomycin is an antibiotic used to treat serious bacterial infections. It is commonly used for infections caused by bacteria called MRSA (methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus) and other hard-to-treat infections. The oral (by mouth) capsule form is specifically used to treat a gut infection called C. difficile (Clostridioides difficile) that causes severe diarrhea. The IV (intravenous) form is used in hospitals to treat serious bloodstream, bone, skin, lung, and other infections.
how_to_take: Oral capsules: Swallow the capsule whole with a full glass of water. You may take it with or without food. If your stomach gets upset, try taking it with food or milk. IV form: This is given through a needle in your vein, usually by a nurse or healthcare provider in a hospital or infusion clinic. Never try to give yourself the IV form at home unless specifically trained to do so. Always finish your full course of vancomycin, even if you start feeling better. Stopping early can allow the infection to come back stronger.
dosing: Your doctor will decide the right dose for you based on your weight, kidney function, and the type of infection you have. Common doses for adults include: Oral capsules for C. diff infection: typically 125 mg taken by mouth 4 times a day for 10 days. IV doses vary widely and are carefully monitored with blood tests. Do not change your dose on your own. Your healthcare team may draw blood regularly to check vancomycin levels and adjust your dose to keep you safe and make sure the medicine is working.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. However, if it is almost time for your next scheduled dose, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular schedule. Do not take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one. If you are receiving vancomycin through an IV and miss an infusion, contact your healthcare provider or infusion nurse right away for instructions.
storage: Oral capsules: Store at room temperature, between 59°F and 86°F (15°C to 30°C). Keep the capsules away from heat, moisture, and direct light. Do not store them in the bathroom. Keep all medications out of reach of children and pets. IV solution prepared at a pharmacy or hospital: Store in the refrigerator and use by the expiration date on the label. Dispose of any unused or expired medication safely. Ask your pharmacist about local drug take-back programs.
what_to_avoid: Avoid taking other medications that can harm your kidneys (such as ibuprofen, naproxen, or certain other antibiotics) without first asking your doctor or pharmacist, as combining these with vancomycin increases the risk of kidney damage. Avoid alcohol while taking vancomycin, as it can add stress to your kidneys and liver. Do not skip doses or stop taking vancomycin early, even if you feel better. Tell your doctor or pharmacist about ALL medications, vitamins, and supplements you are taking before starting vancomycin.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor or seek medical help right away if you experience any of the following: a skin rash, hives, or itching; redness or flushing of your face, neck, or chest (this can happen during IV infusion and is called Red Man Syndrome); swelling of your face, lips, tongue, or throat; difficulty breathing or swallowing; dizziness or feeling faint; ringing in your ears, hearing loss, or changes in hearing; decreased urination, swelling in your legs or feet, or other signs of kidney problems; severe diarrhea that is watery or bloody; pain, swelling, or irritation at the IV injection site; or any new or worsening symptoms.
when_it_works: For IV treatment of serious infections, you may start to feel better within a few days, but blood tests and clinical checks are needed to confirm the medicine is working. For oral treatment of C. diff gut infections, diarrhea usually begins to improve within 2 to 3 days of starting treatment. Always complete the full course of treatment as prescribed, even if symptoms improve quickly. It may take the full course of antibiotics to fully clear the infection.
special_populations: Kidney disease: Vancomycin is removed from your body by your kidneys. If your kidneys do not work well, the drug can build up to harmful levels. Your doctor will check your kidney function and blood vancomycin levels often and adjust your dose as needed. Elderly patients: Older adults are more likely to have reduced kidney function, so closer monitoring is usually needed. Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Tell your doctor if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. Vancomycin should only be used during pregnancy if clearly necessary. It can pass into breast milk in small amounts, so discuss the risks and benefits with your doctor. Children: Doses for children are based on weight and age and must be calculated by a healthcare provider. Hearing and kidney monitoring may be needed in children receiving IV vancomycin.
